title: A Comprehensive Review of AI-based Intelligent Tutoring Systems: Applications and Challenges
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the question of how AI-based Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) function in real educational settings, how effective they are, and what challenges arise in their application and evaluation. The authors note that ITS have shown promise for improving student performance through personalization, adaptive learning, NLP-based interaction, learner modeling, and real-time feedback, but that prior findings are mixed and often methodologically inconsistent.

The intervention studied is not a single ITS program but the broader class of AI-based ITS applications. Using a systematic literature review approach guided by Kitchenham’s recommendations and PRISMA reporting principles, the authors searched major databases including Web of Science, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Springer. They report an initial pool of 37,617 articles, with 127 articles ultimately included for full review, plus 26 specialized web reports. The review examines ITS features, pedagogical strategies, machine learning and NLP integration, student modeling, assessment, domain-specific applications, and implementation challenges.

The population represented across the reviewed studies is mixed, spanning learners in multiple educational contexts and domains rather than one specific age band or sector. Inclusion criteria required empirical studies conducted in real learning environments, in English, with at least 6 weeks of validation and sample sizes of 100 or more. The paper discusses both classroom and online-related uses of ITS, but as a review it synthesizes findings across varied settings rather than evaluating a single implementation context.

The main conclusions are that AI-based ITS can enhance personalized learning, adaptive instruction, engagement, and feedback, with potential benefits across subjects such as mathematics, science, and languages. However, the review emphasizes persistent challenges: inconsistent evaluation methods, limited longitudinal evidence, concerns about transparency, fairness, privacy, and academic integrity, and a need for stronger scientific rigor in experimental design and data analysis. The authors ultimately conclude that ITS are promising but that more rigorous, comparable, and context-sensitive research is needed before strong generalizable claims about effectiveness can be made.

identified_tools.name: ITS
identified_tools.description: AI-based intelligent tutoring systems that provide individualized instruction, guidance, practice, and feedback, often using learner models, adaptive sequencing, natural language interaction, and related AI techniques.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in educational settings to deliver adaptive, personalized tutoring and support student learning, engagement, and instructional decision-making across real-world implementations reviewed in the paper.

findings.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, evidence on the educational effectiveness of AI-based ITS in real-world settings is mixed. Many studies report benefits such as improved learning experiences, personalization, and adaptive support, but heterogeneity in designs, measures, and contexts limits direct comparison and generalizability.
findings.measure: Educational effectiveness and learning outcomes across reviewed ITS studies

findings.finding_summary: The review indicates that AI-based ITS can support personalized learning by adapting content, pacing, and feedback to learner needs, with multiple included studies reporting improved performance or learning support in adaptive environments. However, no pooled quantitative effect size is reported.
findings.measure: Student performance and learning support in personalized/adaptive environments

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that adaptive ITS may improve engagement, motivation, autonomy, and self-regulated learning by adjusting challenge and support to learner progress. It also notes that affect-aware and gamified ITS features may further support engagement and persistence, though results vary by design and context.
findings.measure: Engagement, motivation, autonomy, and self-regulated learning

findings.finding_summary: The review identifies important constraints on broader ITS adoption and evaluation, including insufficient methodological rigor in many studies, inconsistent evaluation metrics, and ongoing concerns about privacy, bias, transparency, fairness, and academic integrity in deployment.
findings.measure: Implementation, evaluation quality, and adoption challenges for ITS deployment

identified_tools.name: Korbit
identified_tools.description: A large-scale dialogue-based intelligent tutoring system and learning platform that uses machine learning and natural language processing to generate personalized instructional support.
identified_tools.use_case: The review cites Kochmar et al. [207] as an example of personalized learning in ITS. Korbit is described as generating automated, data-driven personalized feedback, hints, explanations, and mathematical guidance, dynamically adapting instructional content to a learner’s profile and zone of proximal development using neural networks and reinforcement learning.

findings.finding_summary: Korbit was reported as improving learning by delivering personalized feedback and dynamically adapted instruction aligned to learner needs.

identified_tools.name: iRead
identified_tools.description: An educational technology project/system that integrates explainable AI to support transparent and adaptive learning experiences.
identified_tools.use_case: The review mentions the iRead project in the discussion of explainable AI in ITS. It is presented as an example of how XAI can support personalized learning, classroom diversity management, student engagement, and teacher acceptance by improving transparency and adaptability.

findings.finding_summary: The review states that iRead illustrated how explainable AI can enhance learning outcomes, student engagement, and teacher acceptance, supporting more effective classroom integration of AI.

identified_tools.name: GUIDON
identified_tools.description: An early rule-based intelligent tutoring system developed for teaching medical diagnosis.
identified_tools.use_case: The review lists GUIDON as one of the earliest and most influential rule-based ITS, citing it as an example of a system that used predefined rules and domain knowledge to guide instruction in medical diagnosis.

identified_tools.name: LISP Tutor
identified_tools.description: A classic intelligent tutoring system developed at Carnegie Mellon University to teach LISP programming using a rule-based/cognitive tutoring approach.
identified_tools.use_case: The review names LISP Tutor among early influential rule-based ITS and also includes it in Table 4 as an example of pedagogical strategy implementation. It is discussed as using rule-based and expert-system approaches to support individualized instruction.

identified_tools.name: Andes Physics Tutor
identified_tools.description: A cognitive tutoring system for physics that provides individualized problem-solving support and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The review cites Andes Physics Tutor as a notable example of both rule-based and cognitive tutor approaches. It is described as providing individualized problem-solving support in physics and as a representative cognitive tutor offering personalized feedback and adaptation.

findings.finding_summary: In the review’s summary table, Andes Physics Tutor is associated with physics learning effectiveness through personalized feedback and adaptation.

identified_tools.name: SQL-Tutor
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring system for SQL/database learning that uses rule-based and cognitive tutoring methods to support problem solving.
identified_tools.use_case: The review lists SQL-Tutor as a notable example of both rule-based ITS and cognitive tutors, used to provide individualized problem-solving support in its domain.

identified_tools.name: AutoTutor
identified_tools.description: A dialogue-based intelligent tutoring system that uses natural language processing for question answering and tutorial interaction.
identified_tools.use_case: The review mentions AutoTutor as a notable rule-based ITS and later as a key example in question generation and answering. In Table 4, it is characterized as supporting question generation and answering through NLP and dialogue, with engagement and personalization as key performance targets.

findings.finding_summary: The review states that AutoTutor showed learning gains matching human tutors in question generation and answering contexts, with strong engagement and personalization.

identified_tools.name: CBR-Tutor
identified_tools.description: A case-based reasoning tutoring system that uses prior learning cases to guide instruction in new learner situations.
identified_tools.use_case: The review names CBR-Tutor as an example of case-based reasoning in ITS, using past cases to adapt instruction for new learning scenarios.

identified_tools.name: CBR-Works
identified_tools.description: A case-based reasoning tutoring system used in domains such as software engineering, mathematics, and physics to support problem solving from stored cases.
identified_tools.use_case: The review cites CBR-Works as a notable example of CBR in ITS, describing it as using past cases to guide new learning situations in software engineering, mathematics, and physics.

identified_tools.name: Cognitive Tutor
identified_tools.description: Carnegie Learning’s cognitive tutoring system based on cognitive models that provides step-by-step guidance, adaptive instruction, and feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: The review identifies Carnegie Learning’s Cognitive Tutor as a canonical cognitive tutor and includes it in Table 4 as a system used for scientific learning, emphasizing personalized learning and feedback based on cognitive models and adaptive instruction.

findings.finding_summary: The review characterizes Cognitive Tutor as effective for personalized learning and feedback in real-world educational settings.

identified_tools.name: ACT-R Tutors
identified_tools.description: A family of cognitive-model-based tutoring systems built on the ACT-R framework to provide adaptive, step-by-step instruction.
identified_tools.use_case: The review lists ACT-R Tutors among notable cognitive tutors and in Table 4 describes them as supporting cognitive process understanding and step-by-step guidance through cognitive models and adaptive instruction.

findings.finding_summary: The review summarizes ACT-R Tutors as providing step-by-step guidance and feedback grounded in cognitive process modeling.

identified_tools.name: Electronix Tutor
identified_tools.description: A named cognitive tutoring system mentioned as an example of a domain-specific cognitive tutor.
identified_tools.use_case: The review includes Electronix Tutor in its list of notable cognitive tutors as an example of systems based on cognitive models for domain learning.

identified_tools.name: ITSPOKE
identified_tools.description: An intelligent tutoring spoken dialogue system that combines natural language processing, speech recognition, and tutoring capabilities.
identified_tools.use_case: The review cites Diane et al. [109], describing ITSPOKE as a spoken dialogue tutoring system for physics concepts. It is discussed as enabling spoken tutorial dialogue and multimodal interaction in educational contexts involving conceptual and quantitative physics learning.

identified_tools.name: GPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI large language model used to generate natural-language text, including explanations, responses, and hints via API integration.
identified_tools.use_case: The review discusses GPT and similar LLMs as advancing dialogue systems in ITS by enabling more natural, context-aware responses. It specifically connects GPT to CourseAssist and other LLM-based tutoring systems used for scalable tutoring and interactive learning.

identified_tools.name: CourseAssist
identified_tools.description: An LLM-based tutoring system that adapts GPT-powered question answering for computer science education.
identified_tools.use_case: The review cites Feng et al. [84] and describes CourseAssist as tailoring GPT’s question-answering capabilities to provide effective, scalable tutoring in computer science education.

identified_tools.name: MyLearningTalk
identified_tools.description: A web-based intelligent tutoring system powered by large language models to support dialogue-based interactive learning.
identified_tools.use_case: The review cites [82] and presents MyLearningTalk (MLT) as a dialogue-based ITS powered by LLMs, demonstrating how such models can provide tailored, grounded responses for interactive learning.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic literature review using explicit search procedures, inclusion/exclusion criteria, PRISMA-style reporting, and inter-rater agreement, which supports relatively strong evidence quality. However, it is not a formal meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes, and the authors themselves note methodological inconsistency in the underlying studies.
impact_tier_rationale: The review concludes that ITS show promising but mixed effectiveness, with benefits often reported but not consistently measured or comparable across studies. Because impacts are synthesized narratively without a pooled effect size and the authors highlight unclear generalizability, the overall impact is best characterized as modest or unclear.
